title: Why pancreatic tumours resist KRAS drugs, and a psychedelic phase 3
dek: Interferon signalling emerges as a clue to resistance in pancreatic cancer, a depression drug reports late-stage results with safety questions, and two studies map how autism-linked genes act in the brain.

tldr.text: A study of 242 patient-derived organoids links weak interferon signalling to resistance to KRAS G12D drugs in pancreatic cancer.
A psychedelic depression drug beat placebo in a phase 3 trial, according to the company, while serious adverse events raise safety questions.
Turning up the healthy copy of two autism-linked genes rescued features of human brain organoids, but only in a dish so far.
A 12,434-person trial found lower blood pressure did not significantly cut dementia or mild cognitive impairment in people with diabetes.
NORD opens six rare disease seed grants worth 452,000 dollars in total, with a deadline of 19 January 2027.

top.title: A virus-based bladder cancer treatment cuts recurrence in a phase 3 trial, the company reports
top.gist: CG Oncology says its injected bladder cancer treatment lowered the risk of tumour recurrence by 68 percent in a late-stage trial, according to press coverage of its announcement.

evidence.model: Phase 3 trial, non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
evidence.limitation: A company announcement relayed by the press. Patient numbers, follow-up time and safety data were not available in the articles read for this item.
evidence.conflicts: The result is reported by the company that makes the treatment.

top.why: Late-stage results in earlier bladder cancer help decide whether a treatment can move beyond surgery and surveillance, but only the full data can show how large and durable the benefit is.
top.didNotShow: Not confirmed here: how many patients were treated, how long they were followed, how safe the treatment was, and whether the benefit held in every subgroup.

terms.def: A treatment that uses a virus engineered to infect and kill tumour cells and to draw the immune system to them.

top.title: A psychedelic depression drug beats placebo in phase 3, but safety questions follow
top.gist: Helus Pharma says its lead psychedelic drug improved depression symptoms compared with placebo in a late-stage trial, while press reports note a number of serious adverse events.

evidence.limitation: A company announcement relayed by the press. Effect sizes, patient numbers and the full list of adverse events were not available in the articles read for this item.
evidence.conflicts: The result is reported by the company that makes the drug.

top.why: Psychedelic drugs are reaching late-stage testing, so how serious adverse events are counted and explained will shape whether regulators and clinicians trust the results.
top.didNotShow: Not confirmed here: the size of the benefit, how many people had serious adverse events, and whether those events were judged related to the drug.

top.title: NICE drafts guidance for a swallowable sponge test to find Barrett's oesophagus
top.gist: England's health technology body has drafted guidance recommending a sponge-on-a-thread test to find and monitor Barrett's oesophagus, a condition that can lead to oesophageal cancer.

evidence.model: Draft national guidance based on trial evidence
evidence.limitation: The guidance is a draft still open to consultation. The trial figure is as reported by Cancer Research UK.
evidence.conflicts: Cancer Research UK funded the trials it describes.

top.why: A test given in a GP surgery instead of an endoscopy could widen early detection. The BEST3 trial is reported to have found about ten times more Barrett's cases than current care.

terms.def: A condition in which stomach acid damages the cells lining the food pipe, which can move towards cancer.

top.title: Removing IL-18 slows pancreatic cancer in mice and helps a KRAS drug work
top.gist: In mice that develop pancreatic cancer on their own, deleting the immune signal IL-18 slowed tumours, helped immune cells eat cancer cells and improved the effect of a KRAS-blocking drug.

evidence.model: Genetically engineered mouse models of spontaneous pancreatic cancer
evidence.limitation: Mouse and cell experiments; the abstract does not give group sizes. In people, high IL-18 was only correlated with poorer survival.
evidence.conflicts: Funded by the US National Cancer Institute (NIH).

top.why: Pancreatic tumours are packed with immune-suppressing signals, and showing that one of them hides cancer cells from macrophages gives a possible partner for KRAS drugs.
top.didNotShow: It did not test IL-18 blocking in patients, and it did not show how long the benefit with KRAS drugs lasts.
details: IL-18 acted through STAT1 to raise CD47, a signal that tells macrophages not to eat a cell. Removing IL-18 increased macrophages with stronger antigen-presenting features (more MHCII and CD11c). KRAS inhibitor treatment raised IL-18 in the cancer cells, and deleting IL-18 improved clearance of treated cells.

terms.def: Interleukin-18, an immune signalling protein (a cytokine) of the IL-1 family.
An immune cell that engulfs and digests other cells and debris.
A growth-driving protein that is a main driver of pancreatic cancer.

top.forYou: Relevant to how macrophage activity in dense pancreatic stroma could affect particle uptake and combination design.

top.title: A vaccine against the cancer protein survivin is safe and triggers immunity in a small phase 1
top.gist: In 27 people with advanced lung, ovarian or prostate cancer, a survivin vaccine caused only mild side effects and strong immune responses, but the best tumour response was stable disease.

evidence.limitation: Small, open label, single arm. Immune responses are not proof of benefit, and among 24 evaluable patients the best response was stable disease in 6 (25 percent).
evidence.conflicts: Funded by Oxford Vacmedix UK Ltd, which develops the vaccine.

top.why: Survivin is made by many tumours but the body tends to ignore it, so showing a vaccine can overcome that tolerance is an early step for cancer vaccines.
top.didNotShow: It did not show tumour shrinkage or survival benefit, and it has no comparison group.
details: Related adverse events were all grade 1 to 2. The median anti-survivin antibody titre rose from 20 to a peak of 81,920, and T cell responses (interferon-gamma ELISpot) rose from 16.7 to 504.6 spot-forming units per million cells. Patients with stable disease had higher antibody titres than those whose disease progressed (p = 0.0418). The trial is registered as NCT05104515.

terms.def: A protein made by many tumours that the immune system normally tolerates as 'self'.

top.title: Blood vesicle proteins track how pancreatic cancer responds to FOLFIRINOX
top.gist: In blood samples from 51 people with pancreatic cancer, platelet-related proteins in tiny vesicles fell after FOLFIRINOX but not after gemcitabine-based treatment.

evidence.model: Paired serum samples before and after treatment
evidence.limitation: Not peer reviewed, a small cohort and no validation set described in the abstract. The survival links need replication.
evidence.conflicts: No funding listed in the preprint record.

top.why: Pancreatic cancer lacks good blood tests for treatment response, so a signal that separates two chemotherapy regimens is worth testing in larger groups.
top.didNotShow: It did not test whether the markers can guide treatment choices, and no marker was validated in an independent group.
details: Of the 51 patients, 25 had FOLFIRINOX and 20 had gemcitabine-based therapy. Mass spectrometry found 2,089 vesicle proteins and 26 changed after treatment. Higher ITGB1 before treatment was linked to longer survival (hazard ratio 0.112), and a larger fall in a seven-protein platelet score was linked to shorter survival (hazard ratio 0.56 per unit, p = 0.030).

terms.def: A tiny bubble released by cells that carries proteins and other molecules through the blood.
A combination chemotherapy regimen used for pancreatic cancer.

top.forYou: Relevant to nanoscale vesicle characterisation and liquid biopsy readouts in pancreatic cancer.

top.title: Tau seeds in a once-common Guam brain disease resemble those of CTE
top.gist: Tau protein clumps from people with Guam ALS/PDC, a fatal disease once very common on the island, behave like those of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in a lab test.

evidence.model: Post-mortem brain and spinal cord tissue tested in tau biosensor cells
evidence.limitation: Laboratory tests on post-mortem tissue; the abstract gives no case numbers and does not explain what caused the disease.

top.why: Matching the tau type of a rare disease to a better-studied one gives researchers a shared biology to work from, even though the cause of Guam ALS/PDC is still unknown.
top.didNotShow: It did not identify the cause of the disease or test any treatment.

terms.def: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/parkinsonism-dementia complex, a fatal neurodegenerative disease once very common on Guam.
Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a brain disease marked by deposits of tau protein.
A brain protein that clumps into harmful deposits in several neurodegenerative diseases.
The ability of a small clump of misfolded protein to make normal protein of the same kind clump too.

top.title: A cell-by-cell map points to the striatum as a meeting point of autism biology
top.gist: Single-cell data from the human putamen and a mouse model show gene changes concentrated in one striatal neuron type in autism, with EGR1 and EGR3 as candidate regulators.

evidence.model: 16p11.2 deletion mice, post-mortem human putamen, human striatal organoids
evidence.limitation: The abstract gives no donor numbers. Post-mortem data show association, and deleting EGR1 or EGR3 in organoids reproduced the changes only partly.
evidence.conflicts: Funded by the US NIH Blueprint for Neuroscience Research.

top.why: Autism-linked genes act in many places, so finding where their effects converge can narrow where to look for shared mechanisms.
top.didNotShow: It did not test whether changing these genes affects behaviour or symptoms.

terms.def: Two early growth response genes, which switch on other genes when brain cells are active.
A deep brain region involved in movement and reward; the putamen is part of it.
The main output neuron of the striatum.

top.title: People with schizophrenia and diabetes who start GLP-1 drugs have fewer psychiatric admissions
top.gist: In health records of 70,257 adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes, starting a GLP-1 drug was linked to about a quarter fewer psychiatric hospital admissions than not starting one.

evidence.limitation: Observational, so it cannot show cause; the authors note possible residual confounding and selection bias.
evidence.conflicts: Funded by the SYNDICAT schizophrenia treatment project.

top.why: If a diabetes drug also lowers psychiatric acute care use, it would matter for a group with a high burden of metabolic disease, though trials are needed first.
top.didNotShow: It did not test GLP-1 drugs as a psychiatric treatment, and it did not randomise anyone.
details: The weighted hazard ratio for psychiatric hospitalisation was 0.76 (95 percent interval 0.71 to 0.82) against non-initiation, 0.82 (0.75 to 0.90) against DPP-4 inhibitors and 0.83 (0.78 to 0.88) against SGLT2 inhibitors. For emergency department presentation it was 0.71 (0.65 to 0.77) against non-initiation.

terms.def: How much more or less often an event happens in one group than another; below 1 means less often.
A class of drugs for type 2 diabetes and weight loss.

top.title: EMA committee recommends seven new medicines, including two for lung cancer
top.gist: Europe's medicines committee recommended seven medicines for approval at its November meeting, two of them for non-small cell lung cancer.

evidence.limitation: A regulator's meeting summary; a committee recommendation is not yet a marketing authorisation.

top.why: A CHMP recommendation is the step before the European Commission decides on approval, so it shows what may reach European patients soon.
details: The two cancer medicines are aumolertinib (Aumseqa) and sintilimab (Zybrivo, for non-squamous disease). The other recommendations were for hypertension, diabetes (two insulin aspart biosimilars), a fondaparinux generic and a ruxolitinib generic. None of the seven was for a neurological or psychiatric condition, and none is marked orphan on the page.

terms.def: The European Medicines Agency committee that assesses medicines for human use.

bench.title: KRASG12D-targeted therapy sensitivity depends on interferon signaling activation in pancreatic cancer
bench.headline: Pancreatic tumours that ignore KRAS G12D drugs seem to have switched off interferon signalling.
bench.authors: Zhang Y, Tang S, Zhang Y, et al.

evidence.model: Patient-derived pancreatic cancer organoids and matched tumours
evidence.limitation: Organoid and cell models; the abstract reports no patient treatment outcomes, and the MYC link is described as an association.
evidence.conflicts: Funded by Chinese public bodies including the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

bench.question: Why do some pancreatic cancers with the KRAS G12D mutation not respond to drugs aimed at that mutation?
bench.approach: The authors profiled genes, RNA and proteins across 242 patient-derived organoids and matched tumour tissue, then switched interferon signalling off or on in organoid and cell models.
bench.model: Patient-derived organoids (small tumour-like clusters grown from patient cells) and the tumour tissue they came from.
bench.result: A subset of KRAS G12D tumours was intrinsically resistant and had strongly reduced innate immune signalling. Suppressing interferon made sensitive models resistant; adding interferon beta increased sensitivity, and it acted synergistically with three KRAS inhibitors (MRTX1133, HRS-4642 and RMC-6236). The abstract gives no effect sizes.
bench.limitations: No patient treatment data are reported, effect sizes are not in the abstract, and sustained MYC activity is linked to resistance but not shown to cause it.
bench.meaning: If tumour interferon status predicts response, it could help sort patients for KRAS drugs, and getting interferon-based partners into dense pancreatic tissue becomes a delivery question for carriers.

terms.def: A small three-dimensional culture grown from a patient's tumour cells that keeps some of the tumour's features.
A signalling protein that switches on the body's antiviral and immune defences.

bench.forYou: Relevant to carrying interferon or MYC-targeting agents into dense pancreatic stroma with nanocarriers.

bench.title: Albumin-bound paclitaxel-induced stromal reprogramming drives resistance to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in patients with pancreatic cancer
bench.headline: Chemotherapy changes the fibroblasts around pancreatic tumours in a way that helps the tumour resist it.
bench.authors: Li H, Ma X, Hou X, et al.

evidence.model: Single-cell data from patient tumours plus mouse models
evidence.limitation: The abstract gives no patient numbers. Removing the fibroblast subset in mice shows what the cells do in models, not a drug that can be given to patients.

bench.question: How does albumin-bound paclitaxel plus gemcitabine (AG) change the tissue around a pancreatic tumour, and why do many tumours stop responding?
bench.approach: Single-cell RNA sequencing of patient tumours treated with AG before surgery, then mechanism studies and genetic removal of a fibroblast subset in mouse models.
bench.model: Tumours from patients given neoadjuvant AG and mouse models of pancreatic cancer.
bench.result: AG shifted cancer-associated fibroblasts from a myofibroblast-like (myCAF) to an inflammatory (iCAF) state, and a TMEM100-positive subset was enriched in non-responders. Albumin-bound paclitaxel activated IL-2 STAT5 signalling to raise TMEM100, and those cells released amphiregulin (AREG) that switched on EGFR in tumour cells. Removing TMEM100-positive fibroblasts reversed the shift and improved AG efficacy in mice.
bench.limitations: Patient numbers and effect sizes are not in the abstract, and the targeting was genetic, so no drug against these cells was tested.
bench.meaning: Because albumin-bound paclitaxel is itself a nanoparticle drug, the work shows a carrier's payload can remodel the tissue it must cross, which matters for designing combinations.

terms.def: A supporting connective tissue cell in the tumour stroma that can shield tumour cells.
Given before surgery to shrink or control a tumour.

bench.forYou: Relevant to nanoparticle penetration of dense stroma and how chemotherapy remodels it.

bench.title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism
bench.headline: Switching on the working copy of two autism-linked genes restored gene activity and neuron behaviour in human brain organoids.
bench.authors: Chen GT, Nair G, Osorio AJ, et al.

evidence.model: Human stem-cell-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids
evidence.limitation: Cell and organoid models only, for two genes (CHD8 and SCN2A); no animal or human testing.
evidence.conflicts: Funded by US NIH institutes (NIMH and NICHD).

bench.question: Can turning up the one working copy of a gene correct the effects of losing the other copy?
bench.approach: The authors mapped enhancers (DNA switches) of CHD8 and SCN2A, then used CRISPR-based gene activation aimed at those enhancers in stem-cell-derived neurons and cortical organoids, using the gene's own regulation.
bench.model: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids carrying mutations.
bench.result: The treatment gave a sustained rise in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and organoids, with rescue of expression levels and of mutation-linked changes in gene expression and physiology. The abstract gives no numbers.
bench.limitations: Only two genes and only lab models, the abstract gives no effect sizes, and delivery to neurons in a living brain is not addressed.
bench.meaning: A route for conditions caused by one faulty gene copy: turn up the healthy copy. The reported 15 percent of autism genetic susceptibility from such mutations shows how many genes could be candidates.

terms.def: A problem that arises when one working copy of a gene is not enough.
A stretch of DNA that helps switch a gene on.

bench.title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes
bench.headline: Lower blood pressure targets did not significantly cut dementia or mild cognitive impairment, but brain scans hinted at less damage.
bench.authors: Wang W, Xu Y, Xu F, et al.

evidence.model: Adults aged 50 or older with type 2 diabetes in China
evidence.limitation: Open label with masked outcome assessment, a median follow-up of 3.8 years, and a brain MRI subgroup of only 862 at baseline and 605 at the end.
evidence.conflicts: Funding is not listed in the record.

bench.question: Does a lower blood pressure target reduce dementia, mild cognitive impairment and brain changes in people with type 2 diabetes?
bench.approach: A prespecified secondary analysis of the BPROAD randomised trial: intensive treatment (systolic target below a set level) against standard treatment, with annual cognitive tests and an MRI subset.
bench.model: 12,434 adults without probable dementia from 145 centres, 6,219 assigned to intensive and 6,215 to standard treatment.
bench.result: Systolic pressure at one year was 121.6 against 133.2 mm Hg. Dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 people (3.69 per 100 person-years) against 783 (3.89), hazard ratio 0.96 (95 percent interval 0.86 to 1.06, P = 0.38). In the MRI subgroup, white matter lesion volume grew less with intensive treatment (difference -0.09, interval -0.15 to -0.02, P = 0.01).
bench.limitations: The main outcome was not significantly different, the MRI result is a secondary finding in a subset, and follow-up was under four years.
bench.meaning: Strong blood pressure lowering did not show a clear cognitive benefit within about four years, and the MRI finding needs testing in longer studies.

terms.def: A patch of damage in the brain's wiring tissue seen on MRI, linked to vascular problems.

method.title: Grow patient brain tumour cells inside human brain organoids
method.gist: A published protocol shows how to place patient glioblastoma cells, and optionally patient immune cells, into human cortical organoids to study the tumour in a brain-like setting.
method.useWhen: When you want to test brain tumour cells or their immune interactions in a human brain tissue model for drug screening or mechanism studies lasting about three to four weeks.

steps.title: Process the tumour fast
steps.text: Record the tumour weight, appearance and sample ID, and process the tissue as soon as possible. If you must wait, keep it on ice in sterile medium or at 4 degrees Celsius for up to 12 to 18 hours, accepting progressive loss of viability.

steps.title: Prepare the enzymes
steps.text: Add 5 mL EBSS to the papain bottle and incubate at 37 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes, reconstitute the DNase in 500 microlitres EBSS and add 250 microlitres to the papain. Plan two papain bottles per gram of tumour.

steps.title: Mince and set aside samples
steps.text: Keep the tumour on ice in a 10 cm dish. Before dissociation, set aside tissue for other uses, for example 50 to 100 mg snap frozen for single-nucleus RNA sequencing or about 0.5 cubic centimetres fixed in 4 percent PFA for immunostaining.

steps.title: Dissociate with papain
steps.text: Digest the minced tumour enzymatically with papain to get a single-cell suspension. Optionally label the cells with a fluorescent marker.

steps.title: Transplant onto organoids
steps.text: Place the tumour cells onto mature human cortical organoids (grown from stem cells over 8 to 12 weeks) by the hanging drop method, leaving them overnight.

steps.title: Culture and add immune cells
steps.text: Move the transplanted organoids to multi-well plates. For the immune version, patient peripheral blood mononuclear cells are isolated by density gradient centrifugation. Co-culture lasts 3 to 4 weeks.

pitfalls: Some tumour cell states, such as oligodendrocyte-like cells, are not consistently kept.
Engraftment varies with input tissue quality, including necrosis, bleeding and prior treatment.
The model does not support long-term expansion or serial passaging of tumour cells.
method.safety: Patient tumour tissue and blood are biohazardous human samples that need ethical approval and consent. Follow your institution's biosafety, human tissue and ethics rules, and ask your safety officer if unsure.

terms.def: A culture method in which cells sit in a droplet hanging from a lid so they gather together.
A small three-dimensional tissue culture grown from stem cells that copies some features of an organ.

learn.question: What is the EPR effect, and why is it being rethought?
learn.answer: Early nanomedicine assumed particles pile up in tumours because tumour vessels leak and drain poorly: the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. A 2026 review says that idea came mostly from fast-growing rodent tumours and has translated unevenly to patients.
learn.analogy: A garden hose with holes and a blocked drain: water gets out and stays in the bed. Real tumours may have fewer holes and more mud in between.
body: The idea was that tumour blood vessels have gaps and lymph vessels that drain badly, so nanocarriers about 10 to 200 nanometres wide leak out and stay. The review describes this as the basis of early nanomedicine strategies.

The review argues that EPR was mostly measured in fast-growing subcutaneous rodent tumours, which have higher vessel permeability and lower stromal density than most human tumours. Live imaging in several tumour models suggests particles mostly cross the vessel wall by active transport through cells, called transcytosis, rather than through gaps. The review also cites a median delivery of under 1 percent of the injected dose to tumours.

One response is to make vessels permeable on purpose. In a phase 1 study in metastatic pancreatic cancer, the peptide CEND-1 enhanced delivery of gemcitabine and nanoparticle albumin-bound paclitaxel with acceptable safety, according to the review.

diagram.caption: Simplified route from blood to tumour cell. The review argues each step is less certain in human tumours than in rodent xenografts.

terms.def: A tumour grown in a mouse from human cells.
A cell carrying material across itself in small bubbles.
The supporting tissue around and inside a tumour, made of fibres and non-cancer cells.

sources.label: Review: nanocarriers crossing biological barriers (Int J Pharm X)

trials.title: GLP-1 drug plus standard chemotherapy in metastatic pancreatic, colorectal or liver cancer
trials.what: Tests the safety and feasibility of adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist to standard first-line chemotherapy; the primary outcome is treatment-emergent adverse events.
trials.who: Adults with metastatic pancreatic, colorectal or hepatocellular cancer; 30 planned

trials.title: Liposomal doxorubicin with atezolizumab and or bevacizumab in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer
trials.what: A randomised phase 2/3 trial comparing pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (a chemotherapy drug packaged in a lipid nanoparticle) with atezolizumab, with bevacizumab, or with both.
trials.who: Adults with platinum-resistant recurrent ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer; 444 enrolled

trials.title: Cognitive training with or without psilocybin in aging and Alzheimer's disease (NECTAR)
trials.what: Compares cognitive training alone with cognitive training plus psilocybin; the primary outcome is a neuroplasticity composite score.
trials.who: People aged 65 or older with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer's disease, plus healthy older adults; 200 planned

trials.title: Ketogenic metabolic therapy in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depression
trials.what: A randomised trial of a ketogenic diet with deep omic profiling; primary outcomes are well-being, functioning and quality of life scores.
trials.who: Adults with serious mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depression); 120 planned

funding.title: NORD seed grants for six rare diseases
funding.amount: Up to 50,000 dollars per grant, 152,000 for Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
funding.eligibility: Studies of one of six named diseases, including Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, pheochromocytoma and appendix cancer. The page says only qualified investigators, so read each call.

chatter.title: AACR pancreatic cancer meeting recap highlights RAS drugs and interception
chatter.signal: Over 600 attendees from 18 countries, recap written by a funder of the work
chatter.gist: The recap covers RAS-targeted therapies, mouse work where KRAS blocking cut precancerous lesions, and a talk noting Black patients were 1.7 percent of single-cell samples analysed.

chatter.title: A post on cell replacement trials for Parkinson's disease gets shared
chatter.gist: The post says trials are transplanting lab-grown dopamine-cell precursors, that Japan gave one therapy conditional approval in 2026, and that results are promising but early. It was not checked against a primary source here.

chatter.title: Should you add a batch term in DESeq2 for two sequencing batches?
chatter.signal: #1 of the day's top posts on r/bioinformatics
chatter.gist: A researcher asks whether to add a batch covariate for patient samples sequenced in two batches at the same centre with the same technology.

curiosity.title: Children who practise an instrument score higher on thinking tests, but music may not be the reason
curiosity.gist: In 175 children aged 7 to 9, the 38 who practised an instrument scored higher on intelligence, working memory and reading tests than matched peers.
body: The researchers reused pre-intervention data from a physical activity trial. Trained children were matched to untrained ones by age, sex and family socioeconomic status, with 38 pairs for tests and 25 per group for brain imaging. A possible difference in the right arcuate fasciculus did not hold after correcting for multiple comparisons.
The authors say the design does not allow causal conclusions: families that fund music lessons may offer other enrichment too.

evidence.limitation: Correlational, caregiver-reported training, and no measure of practice intensity. Summarised from a news report of the paper; the paper itself was not read.

note: No job openings are listed today: none could be verified with an open deadline and a stated salary. Company results for the two lead news items come from press coverage, not the full data.
